source: Compiled from NTSB, Wikipedia List of Bermuda Triangle Incidents, and Britannica

incidents.name: USS Cyclops
incidents.details: US Navy cargo ship with 309 crew, disappeared en route from Barbados to Baltimore. No distress signal. Largest non-combat loss of life in US Navy history at the time.
incidents.explanation: Possible structural failure due to overloading (carried manganese ore above rated capacity). Heavy weather documented in area.

incidents.name: Carroll A. Deering
incidents.details: Five-masted schooner found abandoned near Cape Hatteras. Crew of 11 never found. Lifeboats missing, food prepared on stove.
incidents.explanation: Possible mutiny or piracy. Multiple vessels disappeared in same period. FBI investigated rum-running connection.

incidents.name: SS Cotopaxi
incidents.details: Tramp steamer disappeared en route from Charleston to Havana with 32 crew.
incidents.explanation: Wreck identified in 2020 by marine biologist Michael Barnette off St. Augustine, FL. Tropical storm documented on route.

incidents.name: Flight 19
incidents.details: Five TBM Avenger torpedo bombers lost during training flight from Fort Lauderdale. 14 airmen lost. Rescue PBM Mariner also lost (13 crew).
incidents.explanation: Navigation error (compass malfunction documented in radio transcripts). Lt. Taylor refused to switch to emergency frequency. Aircraft ran out of fuel. PBM Mariner likely exploded (known fuel vapor issue).

incidents.name: Star Tiger (G-AHNP)
incidents.details: BSAA Avro Tudor IV disappeared en route from Azores to Bermuda. 31 passengers and crew.
incidents.explanation: Aircraft had known heating system defects. Last radio contact indicated strong headwinds and low fuel. Tudor IV had poor safety record (type later withdrawn from service).

incidents.name: Star Ariel (G-AGRE)
incidents.details: BSAA Avro Tudor IV disappeared en route from Bermuda to Kingston, Jamaica. 20 passengers and crew.
incidents.explanation: Same aircraft type as Star Tiger with same known defects. Entire Tudor IV fleet grounded after this loss. BSAA dissolved.

incidents.name: DC-3 NC16002
incidents.details: Airborne Transport DC-3 charter disappeared en route from San Juan to Miami. 32 passengers and crew. Captain Robert Linquist reported position 50 miles south of Miami.
incidents.explanation: Electrical failure documented (captain reported batteries low). Possible ditching at sea in darkness. Weak signal detected but never confirmed.

incidents.name: SS Marine Sulphur Queen
incidents.details: T2 tanker carrying molten sulphur, disappeared with 39 crew in Straits of Florida.
incidents.explanation: Coast Guard investigation found vessel was structurally deficient (converted from WWII tanker), carrying dangerous cargo without proper safety equipment. Similar T2 tankers had known structural failures.

incidents.name: Witchcraft
incidents.details: 23-foot cabin cruiser reported engine trouble 1 mile off Miami. Coast Guard arrived 19 minutes later, found nothing.
incidents.explanation: Small vessel in open ocean. Many possible explanations including rapid sinking, current drift, or incorrect position report.

incidents.name: Milton Iatrides
incidents.explanation: Hurricane-force winds documented in area at time of disappearance.

incidents.name: SS Sylvia L. Ossa
incidents.details: 590-foot cargo ship disappeared in heavy seas between Bermuda and US coast with 37 crew.
incidents.explanation: Hurricane Lois produced 40-foot seas in the area. Ship was 42 years old.

incidents.name: SS El Faro
incidents.details: 790-foot cargo ship sank near Bahamas with 33 crew during Hurricane Joaquin.
incidents.explanation: NTSB confirmed: captain sailed into hurricane path, vessel flooded and lost propulsion, capsized. Wreck found at 15,000 feet. VDR recovered.

incidents.name: MV Minoan Spirit
incidents.details: Reported missing between Bahamas and Dominican Republic.
incidents.explanation: Vessel found — had communication equipment failure, not a disappearance.

statistical_analysis.source: Lloyd's of London, US Coast Guard
statistical_analysis.finding: The Bermuda Triangle is NOT statistically more dangerous than any comparable area of ocean with similar traffic volume.
statistical_analysis.coast_guard_statement: The Coast Guard does not recognize the Bermuda Triangle as a geographic area of specific hazard to ships or aircraft.
statistical_analysis.lloyds_finding: Lloyd's of London has determined that the triangle is no more dangerous than any other area of ocean and does not charge higher rates for passage through the region.

debunking_sources.author: Larry Kusche
debunking_sources.title: The Bermuda Triangle Mystery — Solved
debunking_sources.finding: Investigated each reported incident individually. Found most were misreported, exaggerated, or had documented explanations (storms, mechanical failure). Many incidents occurred outside the triangle's boundaries.

debunking_sources.author: NOVA/PBS
debunking_sources.title: The Case of the Bermuda Triangle
debunking_sources.finding: Documentary concluded no unusual phenomena. Weather patterns, human error, and Gulf Stream explain incidents.

debunking_sources.author: Benjamin Radford
debunking_sources.title: Skeptical Inquirer analysis
debunking_sources.finding: Number of incidents not disproportionate to traffic volume. Cherry-picking creates false pattern.
